entries.modern_form: Arabic ال al- , the definite article 'the', proclitic and inseparable; assimilated to a following 'sun letter' (t, ṯ, d, ḏ, r, z, s, š, ṣ, ḍ, ṭ, ẓ, l, n): al-šams > aš-šams
entries.note: The root box is right on all three counts: the language label (Arabic), the form (al- used as a prefix) and the gloss ('definite article "the"'), and its printed note about assimilation is the standard sun-letter rule, which Persian grammars teach unchanged (Platts–Ranking §10, 'solar letters … lunar letters'). Nourai's added remark that 'most of these Arabic words have reached Europe through Spanish and French' is also correct and is confirmed word by word by Klein, Devic and Lokotsch — though the carriers are wider than Spanish and French alone (Italian for arsenal and lute, Portuguese for albatross and anil, Catalan for aubergine and apricot). Three problems in the chart itself: (1) 'Amir al-bahr' as the source of admiral is rejected by Klein (who prefers amīr-ar-raḥl), by Devic (who attributes it to Engelmann and calls it 'guère admissible') and by Lokotsch ('wenig wahrscheinlich'); the OED accepts only the generic amīr-al-. (2) 'az-zarnîx : arsenic' is a real Arabic word but not the source of European arsenic — Greek arsenikon was taken from Iranian *zarnika- through Syriac zarnīkā centuries before Arabic, and Latin/Old French carried it to English; Watkins (AHD, root *ghel-2) says 'Syriac zarnikā, orpiment: ARSENIC'. (3) 'aloe' under al-oud is wrong — aloe is Greek ἀλόη of uncertain, probably Semitic-or-Dravidian ancestry, and Nourai's own cross-reference ☞Agaruth (Sanskrit agaru) points at that different etymology; 'flute' on the same line is at best a blend with laüt 'lute', not a descendant of al-ʿūd. Everything else on the page is standard and well supported. The Persian script of the page was checked against the page image (pdftoppm p.47): «آلفا آلفا» for âlfâlfâ really is printed as two words in the book, so the JSON is a faithful transcription and no transcription_suspect verdict is warranted.

nodes.derivation: Persian has no definite article of its own; what it has are whole Arabic phrases taken over unanalysed with ال al- still attached. الله allāh < al-ilāh 'the god' (the ه of the Persian pronunciation allâh is the Arabic form exactly); الکل al-koll 'the whole, the totality' (Arabic al-kull, the abstract used in Persian philosophical/administrative idiom, e.g. الکل فی الکل); المثنّی al-mothannā 'the doubled one, the dual' (passive participle of Arabic ثنّى thannā 'to double', also a proper name). In all three the article is inseparable in Persian: Persian speakers never strip the al- and never inflect it, which is exactly Nourai's point in the root box. Note that الکل here is al-koll 'the all', not the alcohol word of node #8 (Persian alkol, from French), although the two are written identically.

nodes.derivation: Two Arabic al- phrases. (1) أمير البحر amīr al-baḥr 'commander of the sea': amīr is the active participle of أمر amara 'to command' (Nourai's ☞A`.m.r), baḥr 'sea'. The word really did reach Europe as an Arabic amīr + article, but the specific phrase is contested: the OED explains that 'as amīr is constantly followed by -al- in all such titles, amīr-al- was naturally assumed by Christian writers as a substantive word', and Klein prefers amīr-ar-raḥl 'commander of transport'. Devic reports the amīr al-baḥr guess as Engelmann's and rejects it, Lokotsch calls it 'wenig wahrscheinlich'. So the al- is genuine, the baḥr is not established — hence 'plausible' rather than 'confirmed'. (2) فصفصة al-fiṣfiṣa / al-faṣfaṣa 'lucerne, green fodder' is itself an Iranian loan in Arabic: Middle Persian aspast (asp 'horse' + -ast 'food', PIE *h₁ed- 'eat' + *h₁eḱwo- 'horse' — Nourai's ☞Ed, Ekwos), whence Andalusian Arabic al-fáṣfaṣa and Spanish alfalfa (earlier alfalfez). Nourai's gloss 'horse food' is literally Watkins's gloss for the Iranian compound.

nodes.derivation: admiral: Middle English amiral/admirail 'Saracen commander' c.1200, from Old French amirail (12c.), itself from Medieval Latin amiratus/admiralis, a title that acquired its naval sense in 12th-c. Norman Sicily; 'amiral de la mer' appears in late-13c. Anglo-French, and the sense 'highest naval officer' is early-15c. English. The unetymological -d- is from Latin admirari 'to wonder at' (whence admire). So the al- is Arabic, but as the frozen tail of amīr-al-, not demonstrably from baḥr. alfalfa: borrowed into American English in 1845 from Spanish alfalfa (earlier alfalfez) < Andalusian Arabic al-fáṣfaṣa < Classical Arabic fiṣfiṣa < Middle Persian aspast; the plant is the European 'lucerne', renamed in the New World from the Spanish form.

nodes.derivation: Modern Persian technical loans that re-enter Persian from the West, closing Nourai's Arabic → Europe → Persian loop. آدمیرال âdmirâl 'admiral' is taken from English/French admiral–amiral (the -d- shows it is the Western, not the Arabic, form; a direct Arabic borrowing would be امیرالبحر amir-al-bahr, which Persian also has as دریاسالار's Arabic equivalent). Mo'in glosses آدمیرال precisely by that Arabic phrase. آلفالفا 'alfalfa' is a 20th-c. re-borrowing of the Spanish/English name for a plant Persian already had as یونجه yonje — a genuine round trip, since the Arabic word behind alfalfa is itself from Middle Persian aspast. Caveat: the book prints the Persian of the second word as two separate words, «آلفا آلفا» (verified on the page image, pdftoppm p.47), i.e. âlfâ âlfâ, which does not match its own transliteration âlfâlfâ and is not the normal Persian spelling آلفالفا; and neither آلفالفا nor آلفا آلفا is in the Mo'in text on disk. Hence 'plausible' rather than 'confirmed'.

nodes.derivation: Three al- forms that fed medieval Latin science. (1) الكحل al-kuḥl (vulgar al-kohl; Nourai's 'al-kahl' renders the root vowel of كحل k-ḥ-l, his ☞K.h.l) is the impalpable powder of antimony sulphide used as eye-paint; the sense 'highly rectified spirit' that Nourai glosses is the later European development, from Paracelsus's use of the word for anything reduced to its finest essence. (2) الخوارزمي al-Khwārizmī 'the man of Khwārazm' (modern Khiva), nisba of Abū Jaʿfar Muḥammad b. Mūsā, the Baghdad mathematician of the 9th c. whose Kitāb al-jabr wa-l-muqābala gave Europe both 'algebra' and, from his name, 'algorism/algorithm'; the al- is the article of the nisba. Nourai's ☞Ghdhem points at the Iranian place-name element. (3) الإثمد al-ithmid (also uthmud) 'stibnite, antimony', a metathesised borrowing of Coptic ⲉⲥⲑⲏⲙ esthēm / Greek στίμμι stímmi, ultimately Egyptian sdm.

nodes.derivation: The empty box stands for the Medieval Latin of the translators and alchemists, which is where all three words of node #5 actually entered Europe: ML alcohol / alcofol 'powdered ore of antimony' (Paracelsus, d.1541, extends it to any sublimate and to volatile liquids); ML algorismus (12th-c. Latin versions of al-Khwārizmī's arithmetic, Liber algorismi de numero Indorum, with the second syllable pulled toward Greek ἀριθμός arithmos); ML antimonium (11th c.), a heavy Latin mangling of al-ithmid. The 12th–13th c. Toledo translation workshops are the concrete channel.

nodes.derivation: French alcool, algorithme, antimoine. French refashioned Old French algorisme into algorithme under the mistaken pull of Greek arithmos 'number'; antimoine acquired in French the joke folk-etymology anti-moine 'monk's bane'. This French stage is the one that matters for node #8, because modern Persian took all three words from French, not from Latin or Arabic.

Devic's whole book is the French reception of these Arabic words; s.v. Alcool he gives 'Esp. et portug. alcohol, aragon. alcofol, catal. alcofoll' as the Iberian stage feeding French alcool.
Etymology tree: 'Egyptian sdm → Ancient Greek στίμμι → Coptic ⲉⲥⲑⲏⲙ → Arabic إِثْمِد → Latin antimonium → French antimoine → Persian آنتیموان' — the French link is explicit.

nodes.derivation: All three are 19th–20th c. Persian borrowings from French, as their phonetic shape shows. الکل alkol keeps the French -ool of alcool (a direct Arabic borrowing would have given kohl/kuḥl without the article, as Persian کحل kohl in fact does); آنتیموان ântimo'ân is French antimoine with the nasal rendered -oân; آلگوریتم âlgoritm is French algorithme, with the Greek-influenced -ith- that only the French form has (Arabic and Latin had algorism-). The last word is an especially neat round trip: al-Khwārizmī was an Iranian from Khwārazm, so the Persian word is his own name returned after a thousand years by way of Baghdad, Toledo and Paris.

nodes.derivation: The three English words are right, but Nourai's single Latin→English arrow flattens three different routes. alcohol really is a direct Medieval Latin borrowing (1540s, earlier alcofol early 15c., 'fine powder produced by sublimation'; 'intoxicating ingredient' only by 1753, short for alcohol of wine). antimony is early 15c. from Old French antimoine AND directly from ML antimonium — so French is in the chain, not bypassed. algorithm is not from Latin at all in its modern shape: Middle English had algorism (early 13c.) from Old French algorisme, and the -ith- form is a 1690s borrowing of French algorithme; so English inherits the French refashioning, which Nourai's chart routes only to Persian. Hence 'plausible': right words, over-simplified arrow.

nodes.derivation: (1) القلي al-qilī 'the calcined ashes of the saltwort (Salsola), rich in soda', from قلى qalā 'he roasted, fried' — Nourai's gloss is exactly right and the word is the source of alkali. (2) المالغم al-malgham 'soft mass, emollient poultice', which Arabic itself took (via Syriac malagmā) from Greek μάλαγμα malagma 'softening substance' — right, and Nourai's ☞Mel 3 points at PIE *mel- 'soft'. (3) الزرنيخ az-zarnīkh 'orpiment, arsenic' is a genuine Arabic word and genuinely Iranian in origin (Middle Persian zarnīk 'golden', OP *daraniya- 'gold', Nourai's ☞Ghel = PIE *ǵʰel- 'to shine, yellow') — but it is NOT the source of European 'arsenic'. Greek ἀρσενικόν arsenikon (Dioscorides, 1st c. CE, reshaped by folk etymology after ἄρσην 'male') was borrowed from Iranian through Syriac ܙܪܢܝܟܐ zarnīkā some six centuries before Arabic existed as a literary language, and Latin arsenicum > Old French arsenic > English arsenic descends from the Greek. The az- of Nourai's chart is the Aramaic/Syriac, not the Arabic, definite state. That is why this node is 'disputed'.

nodes.derivation: French alcali, arsenic, amalgame. Two of the three sit correctly on an Arabic parent: alcali is first found in Albertus Magnus's Latin (alkali) and is French alcali/alcalli by the 16th c.; amalgame is French from Medieval Latin amalgama, an alchemists' word for a mercury alloy, itself dissimilated from al-malgham. The third, arsenic, is French only in the sense that Old French arsenic continues Latin arsenicum from Greek — it does not descend from the Arabic box above it, so this pass-through box inherits node #10's problem for one of its three words.

nodes.derivation: Both are modern chemical loans from French: آلکالی âlkâlî < French alcali (Persian's older, Arabic-mediated word for the same substance is قلیا qalyā, straight from al-qilī, which is what makes the French form recognisably a second, Western borrowing), and آرسنیک ârsenik < French arsenic. The Persian→French step Nourai draws is correct for both; what is wrong is only the ancestry he assigns to arsenic above node #11, since French arsenic comes from Latin/Greek and not from Arabic az-zarnīkh — Persian's genuinely inherited word for the same substance is زرنیخ zarnīkh, which Borhān-e Qāṭeʿ still lists. Neither Persian form is in the Moʿin text available on disk, and Nourai's only reference here (VOP) is unobtainable, so the node cannot be raised above 'plausible'.

nodes.derivation: alkali is late 14c. English 'soda ash', from Medieval Latin alkali < Arabic al-qilī, with alkaline a 1670s English derivative in -ine — confirmed. amalgam is c.1400, from Old French amalgame or directly from ML amalgama (c.1300, an alchemists' word), probably from al-malgham — confirmed. arsenic, however, is late 14c. from Old French arsenic < Latin arsenicum < late Greek arsenikon, adapted from Syriac (al-)zarniqā < Middle Persian zarnīk 'gold-coloured'; the word entered Greek from Iranian through Aramaic in antiquity and never passed through Arabic, so listing it as an al- word is a mistake — the al/az- in the Syriac form is the Aramaic determinate state, not the Arabic article. Because the chart makes arsenic a descendant of the Arabic definite article, the node is disputed.

nodes.derivation: Five al- forms, four of them exported. الله Allāh is a contraction of al-ilāh 'the god' (Nourai's ☞Layh = the Semitic ʾ-l-h stem, cognate with Aramaic ʾelāh, Hebrew ʾĕlōah). القادوس al-qādūs is the pot or bucket of a water-wheel (< Greek κάδος kados 'jar', itself a Semitic loan, Hebrew kad); it named the pelican 'the water-carrier' (compare Arabic saqqā 'pelican', literally 'water carrier'), whence Portuguese alcatruz > alcatraz > albatross. الأنبيق al-anbīq 'the still, the cap of a still' is Greek ἄμβιξ ambix taken over with the article, reaching Europe through Old Spanish alambique. الباذنجان al-bādhinjān is a Persian loan in Arabic (Classical Persian bādingān/bāzingān < Sanskrit vātiṅgaṇa < Dravidian — exactly Nourai's ☞Vatin-ganah). النيل al-nīl 'the indigo' is likewise Persian nīl < Sanskrit nīlī 'indigo', nīla- 'dark blue'.

nodes.words: Allah; albatross; alembic; aubergine; anil, aniline
nodes.derivation: Allah entered English in 1702 (Alha) directly from Arabic as a religious term. albatross, 1670s, is an alteration (after Latin albus 'white', for the bird's plumage) of Spanish/Portuguese albatros < alcatraz 'pelican, cormorant', from al-qādūs; OED prints Nourai's al-qādūs route, Barnhart prefers al-ghaṭṭās 'the diver', so Nourai has picked the better-documented of the two. alembic is late 14c. (earlier limbeck mid-14c.) from Old French alambic < Old Spanish alambique < al-anbīq. aubergine, 1775, is French aubergine < Catalan alberginera (the regular French change of al- to au-) < al-bādhinjān. anil is 1580s from Portuguese/French anil < an-nīl (assimilated al-nīl), and aniline is a chemical coinage of 1841 (C. J. Fritzsche) on anil + -ine. The chart's straight Arabic→English arrows compress the Iberian, French and Portuguese intermediaries, but the root box itself says so ('Most of these Arabic words have reached Europe through Spanish and French').

nodes.words: al-iksir; al-a`sârah; al-jabr-w`al- moqâbeleh; al-kîmîyâ; al-oud
nodes.derivation: Five al- forms of the Arabic scientific vocabulary. الإكسير al-iksīr 'the philosophers' stone, the dry medicine' is late Greek ξηρίον xērion 'drying powder for wounds' (from ξηρός xēros 'dry' — Nourai's ☞Ksero) taken over with the article. العصارة al-ʿaṣāra 'the pressed-out juice', from عصر ʿaṣara 'he squeezed' (☞A`.s.r), was the Levantine trade name of madder root (alizari) and gave the dye name alizarin. الجبر والمقابلة al-jabr wa-l-muqābala 'restoration and balancing' is the title of al-Khwārizmī's treatise, al-jabr from جبر jabara 'to set (a bone), reunite' (☞J.b.r) — which is why Spanish algebrista still means 'bone-setter'. الكيمياء al-kīmiyāʾ is from Greek χημεία khēmeia, itself of contested origin: either Egyptian khem/kēme 'the black land' (Nourai's ☞Kers 2) or χεῖν khein 'to pour' (☞Gheu); Nourai cites both, which is the honest position, though Klein calls the second folk etymology. العود al-ʿūd 'the wood' is the Arab lute; the aloewood sense of ʿūd is why Nourai cross-refers ☞Agaruth (Sanskrit agaru 'aloewood').

nodes.words: elixir; alizarin; algebra; alchemy, chemistry; lute, flute, aloe
nodes.derivation: Four of the five lines are right. elixir, mid-13c., from ML elixir < al-iksīr. alizarin, from French alizarine (1830s–50s dye chemistry) = alizari + -in, alizari being the Levantine madder trade-name from al-ʿaṣāra. algebra, 1550s, from ML algebra < al-jabr (the accent moved from the second to the first syllable in the 17th c.; English also used algebra for 'bone-setting' in the 15th–16th c., from Arab medical men in Spain). alchemy, mid-14c., from Old French alquemie/alchimie < ML alkimia < al-kīmiyāʾ, with chemistry a c.1600 back-formation on chemist (French chimiste < ML alchimista, the al- shed). lute, late 13c., from Old French lut/leüt < Old Provençal laut, 'a misdivision of Arabic al-ʿūd … where al is the definite article'. But the last two words of the last line do not belong: flute (early 14c. floute, OF flaüte, OProv flaüt) is of uncertain origin — perhaps imitative, perhaps from Latin flare 'to blow' — and is at most 'influenced by' or blended with laüt 'lute' (Klein: 'prob. a blend of OProvenç. flaujol "flageolet" and laüt "lute"'), not descended from al-ʿūd. aloe is not an Arabic al- word at all: it is Latin aloe < Greek ἀλόη, of uncertain (probably Oriental) origin, with the older English 'fragrant heartwood' sense coming from the Biblical translators' use of aloe for Hebrew ʾăhālīm, ultimately perhaps Dravidian (Sanskrit agaru — which is exactly what Nourai's own ☞Agaruth points at, so his cross-reference contradicts his arrow). Because two words of the node are wrongly filiated to al-, the node is disputed.

nodes.derivation: Five more al- exports, three of them showing the assimilation the root box describes. البرقوق al-birqūq/al-barqūq is Byzantine Greek βερικόκκιον berikokkion, itself Latin (mālum) praecoquum 'early-ripening (fruit)' (Nourai's ☞Pekw = PIE *pekʷ- 'to cook, ripen'); his parenthesis '(plum)' is exact, because modern Arabic barqūq means 'plum', the apricot being mishmish. دار الصناعة dār aṣ-ṣināʿa 'house of manufacture' (☞S.n.`a, D.v.r) shows al- assimilated to ṣ before a sun letter — Nourai's 'dr-as-sanâ' is the book's shorthand for it. السموت as-sumūt, plural of السمت as-samt 'the way, direction' (☞Mei 3), again with sun-letter assimilation. جبل طارق Jabal Ṭāriq 'mountain of Ṭāriq', after Ṭāriq b. Ziyād, who landed there in 711 and opened the conquest of Spain (☞J.b.l 'mountain'); note that the received Arabic name has no article between the two words, so the al- Nourai writes is Klein's citation form rather than standard Arabic. القبة al-qubba 'the vault, vaulted chamber, vaulted tent', from the Semitic base q-b-b 'to be bent, vaulted' (☞Gabbah).

nodes.derivation: apricot, 1550s abrecock, from Catalan abercoc / Portuguese albricoque < al-birqūq, the modern form assimilated to French abricot; the fruit was introduced to England in 1524. arsenal, c.1500 'dockyard, dock with naval stores', from Italian arzenale (Venetian arzanà, the great Arsenale of Venice) < dār aṣ-ṣināʿa; the sense 'store of weapons' is 1570s. azimuth, late 14c., from Old French azimut < as-sumūt (its doublet zenith comes from the singular samt ar-raʾs, with -m- misread as -ni- by Latin scribes). Gibraltar, 1590s, from Jabal Ṭāriq, ancient Calpe. alcove, 1670s, from French alcôve < Spanish alcoba < al-qubba. Nourai's direct Arabic→English arrows again pass over the Italian, Iberian and French carriers, which the root box's own note covers.
